newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire provinces brace for looting by army.
newsitem.headline: Zaire provinces brace for looting by army.

text.p: Authorities in Zaire's shrinking number of government-held provinces are bracing for possible looting by Zairean soldiers fleeing advancing rebels, local politicians said on Friday.

Dignitaries from Bandundu Province, Zaire's western bread basket which is in the path of rebels closing in on Kinshasa, discussed their fears with Prime Minister Likulia Bolongo on Wednesday in the national capital.
They told Reuters on Friday that "emergency committees" comprising civilians and military members had been set up in towns across the province.

A spokesman for the group hinted that the local population would be happy to welcome Laurent Kabila's rebels who have already seized more than half Zaire's vast territory in their six-month-old campaign to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko.
"The (Bandundu) population is more concerned about army-led looting than anything else," spokesman Kamitatu Masamba said.

The Kinshasa daily, Le Soft, founded by Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba, said on Friday that panic-stricken people were fleeing Kikwit, the Bandundu town which was propelled into the world limelight by an epidemic of the Ebola virus in 1995.
However, Kamitatu, who is in frequent radio contact with Kikwit, cast doubt on the report.
"I last spoke to my people in Kikwit this morning, but nobody told me the population was fleeing the town," he said.

The newspaper also said Kikwit was being reinforced to become the Zaire army's forward headquarters to resist the rebels. That role was played by the eastern city of Kisangani until it was captured by rebels in mid-March, despite the presence of foreign mecenaries backing the army there.
A Bandundu politician, who asked not to be named, told Reuters that local youth were already in touch with the rebels.
"The Bandundu youth even sent a delegation to Kananga to tell the rebels to capture this province as quickly as possible," he said.
Zaire's unruly and unpaid soldiers have been far more inclined to looting than fighting. Deserting troops have terrorised and pillaged towns and villages as they fled the warzone in the east.
"The emergency committee wants to get the soldiers who are in Bandundu to leave the province, but they are afraid of being disarmed if they arrive in Kinshasa," Kamitatu said.
The fear of looting has spread to Zaire's port city of Matadi on the Atlantic coast, where many shopowners have kept away most merchandise in secure warehouses.
